subcategory: limestone cedar glade and barrens endemic

planting.note: Nick or lightly sand the hard seed coat and direct sow in fall onto thin, rocky, alkaline soil so winter freeze-thaw cycles complete stratification; like other milkvetches it develops a deep taproot early and resents any later transplanting.

directions: Tennessee milkvetch is a low, spreading-to-ascending perennial legume centered on the limestone cedar glades and adjacent barrens of Middle Tennessee's Central Basin, with scattered disjunct populations on similar calcareous glade and barren openings in Kentucky, Alabama, and Georgia. Its pinnately compound leaflets carry a dense silvery-silky pubescence that gives the whole plant a soft gray-green cast, a trait shared with many other true glade legumes. In mid-to-late spring it produces dense, short racemes of cream to pale yellowish-white pea flowers held just above the foliage, followed by inflated, bladder-like seed pods typical of the genus. Grow it exactly as you would other glade specialists such as Dalea gattingeri or Echinacea tennesseensis: on exposed limestone rubble or very thin, lime-rich soil with no mulch, amendment, or supplemental irrigation, since excess fertility and moisture both shorten its life in cultivation.
